tags.name: analytics
tags.description: What an organiser’s events actually did: tickets gone, seats left, people admitted, refunds and disputes outstanding, and the money behind all of it. Every figure is counted from the record it belongs to — money from the append-only ledger, inventory from the seats themselves — and a measurement this system does not record is named as missing rather than estimated.

tags.description: Money leaving: what an organiser is owed, what is held against it, and the payouts, transfers and disputes that move it. Every figure is derived from the append-only ledger rather than read off a column, and a reversal posts compensating entries rather than editing history.

tags.name: refunds
tags.description: Giving money back: requesting, approving, submitting and withdrawing. Every amount is computed from the order, every step is audited, and the provider is called with no transaction open — a refund is the one commerce action where every failure mode costs somebody money.

tags.name: privacy
tags.description: Redacting a person’s personal data, and the record of having done it. Organisation-scoped and never platform-wide: one request names one subject inside one organisation. Redaction is irreversible — no reversal path, original value, encrypted copy or recoverable mapping is stored — so every command here needs the narrow `privacy:redact` capability, a step-up no older than two minutes, and a single-use confirmation the server issued. Nothing on this surface returns a value that was or will be redacted: a request is described by counts and categories, and the subject by an opaque id.

post.description: Exchange email and password for a session, returned both as a cookie and as a bearer token carrying the same secret. A wrong password and an unknown email answer identically, and both pay the same hashing cost, so neither the body nor the response time enumerates accounts. An account with a second factor and no code supplied answers 200 with `mfaRequired` rather than an error — an error would have to distinguish "wrong password" from "right password, now show a code", which tells an attacker which passwords are correct. Failures are counted per address and per source, and a caller past either threshold gets 429 with no indication of which counter tripped.

get.description:
Everybody in this organisation, the invitations still outstanding, and the roles the caller may grant. The role list is computed from what the caller holds rather than fixed, because a member cannot grant a power they do not have. Carries each person's name and nothing else about their account. Addresses are decided by the server and carried in one of three shapes told apart by `emailVisibility`. `FULL` needs `team:role_manage` held through the caller's own membership of this organisation (ADMIN, OWNER) and a second factor confirmed within the `MEMBER_EMAIL_VIEW` step-up window. `STEP_UP_REQUIRED` is the same caller without that recent confirmation: no addresses, and a step-up followed by a second request will show them. `HIDDEN` is everybody else who may read the list (MANAGER, EVENT_MANAGER, FINANCE, STAFF, VIEWER, and a platform super administrator who is not a member): no address field at all, and names carrying an address have it replaced with `Hidden email`. SCANNER cannot read the list. `assignableRoles` lists only roles that neither create nor publish events (FINANCE, STAFF, SCANNER, VIEWER, bounded by what the caller holds): roles that post events are given by the Desi-Event team. Each member carries `postsEvents`, and `roleChoices`, the roles this caller may move that member to — empty for the caller and for an owner, and a posting role only downwards for somebody who already posts.

Requires the `organization:view_members` capability.

post.description:
Issue a single-use invitation code for an email address, for a role bounded by what the caller holds: a member cannot invite somebody to a role that carries powers they lack, and OWNER cannot be invited at all. Roles that create or publish events (event manager, manager, administrator) are given by the Desi-Event team, and inviting somebody to one answers 403 `POSTING_ROLE_NEEDS_PLATFORM` with nothing written. An address that already belongs to the organisation answers 409. A second invitation to the same address supersedes the first, and the database holds at most one live invitation per address, so two issued at the same moment produce one invitation and one 409. How the code reaches the invitee is the deployment’s `DELIVERY_MODE`. In `MANUAL`, the default, `data.delivery.invitationCode` carries the code, returned exactly once, in this 201 only, with `cache-control: no-store, private`; it is never logged or audited, and only its SHA-256 digest is stored, so nobody can show it again. The inviter hands it over themselves. In `EMAIL` (`DELIVERY_MODE=EMAIL` with an SMTP server configured) the mail server sends it, `invitationCode` is null, and an address that has already been sent three codes from Desi-Event in the last day answers 429 `RECIPIENT_DAILY_LIMIT`; if the server refuses the message, the invitation is withdrawn and the answer is 503 `DELIVERY_FAILED`, so no code is left live that nobody holds.

Requires the `team:invite` capability.

post.description: Join an organisation with an invitation code, typed rather than followed from a link. The caller must be signed in as the address the invitation names — a code passed on to somebody else does not work for them, which is what stops an invitation becoming a transferable key, and the refusal names no part of that address. Single-use, enforced by a conditional update, so two simultaneous acceptances produce one membership. Joining is a privilege change (finding NF-10): every other session the caller holds ends, a cookie session is given a new secret, and the session is shortened to the privileged lifetime when the new role is privileged. `data.joined` is false when the account already belonged to the organisation: the code is spent, the existing role is unchanged and no session ends. `data.session` says whether the account now needs a second factor and whether it has one. A direct grant that adds the account at the same moment answers 409 and leaves the code usable. An invitation that offers a role which creates or publishes events (one written before such invitations were withdrawn) answers 403 `POSTING_ROLE_NEEDS_PLATFORM` and is not spent, and an organiser invitation code answers 403 `WRONG_INVITATION_KIND` and is not spent either. Rate limited per account.

post.summary: Issue a new code for an invitation
post.description:
For a code that was lost, never handed over, or issued before codes were shown to the inviter. The outstanding invitation is withdrawn and a new one is issued for the same address and role in one transaction, so the old code stops working at the moment the new one exists. Bounded like an invitation: the caller must be able to grant the invitation’s role, so a MANAGER cannot obtain a code for a FINANCE invitation an owner issued. Keyed by the invitation, because a caller who may not see addresses cannot retype one. The new code is returned exactly as `teams.invite` returns one: once, with `cache-control: no-store, private`, never logged or audited; in `EMAIL` it is sent, with the same daily limit per address and the same withdrawal and 503 `DELIVERY_FAILED` when the mail server refuses it. An invitation offering a role that creates or publishes events answers 403 `POSTING_ROLE_NEEDS_PLATFORM`. An invitation that is no longer outstanding answers 409, and one belonging to another organisation 404.

Requires the `team:invite` capability.

post.description:
The only way an owner stops being one and somebody else starts, done as one swap: the named member becomes OWNER and the caller becomes ADMIN, in one transaction with the owners locked, so there is never a moment with no owner or a second one nobody meant. Only an OWNER of this organisation may do it, through their own membership — a platform super administrator uses the audited direct grant instead. Requires a second factor confirmed within the SECURITY_ROLE window. The new owner’s sessions all end, so they sign in again under the role they now hold; the caller’s cookie session is given a new secret. The caller cannot name themselves (403), and a membership of another organisation, or one removed while the transfer waited, is not found (404) and nothing changes. The heir must already create events here — an event manager, manager or administrator — or the answer is 422 `HEIR_MUST_POST_EVENTS`, so a transfer never makes somebody new a poster of events.

Requires the `organization:manage` capability.

Requires a recent step-up authentication: see `POST /v1/auth/step-up`.

patch.description:
Bounded three ways. The caller must be able to grant the new role and must already hold power over the old one, so nobody can promote somebody past themselves or demote somebody above them. Nobody may change their own role, which is what stops a MANAGER making themselves an ADMIN. And the last OWNER cannot be demoted: an organisation with no owner is one nobody can fix. Each of these is decided from the member’s role as it stands once their row and the owners’ are locked, so an ownership transfer landing at the same moment cannot turn a permitted change into the demotion of an owner. A role that creates or publishes events is set only on a member who already holds one, and only downwards (to a role whose powers are a subset of theirs); any other move to such a role answers 403 `POSTING_ROLE_NEEDS_PLATFORM`, because who posts events is decided by the Desi-Event team.

Requires the `team:role_manage` capability.

Super administrators (`platform:admin`) only, with a second factor confirmed within the SECURITY_ROLE window. Never the caller’s own account (403). Every session the account holds ends in the same transaction, so it signs in again under the new role — and a privileged role must then set up a second factor before it can work.

post.summary: Look a group pass up at the door
post.description: Resolves a group pass — its scanned QR or its printed `DEG-` code — and lists every ticket on the order that its buyer still holds, each with the same outcome and closed refusal reason a single lookup gives, plus counts and how many tickets from the order were handed to other people. Writes nothing to any ticket. The same door authority as a single ticket, checked against the order's own event from the database; a caller not authorised for it gets the same 404 as a caller who presented nothing real. Each ticket names its night (`session`), and the door names the night it is admitting to (`eventSessionId`) on an event of more than one, as for a single ticket: a ticket for another night is refused `WRONG_NIGHT`. When at least one ticket is admissible the answer carries a short-lived `previewReference` naming them and the night, bound to this scanner and this way of presenting, which a group confirmation must return. Rate-limited per scanner, never cached, and neither the pass, the code nor the reference is ever logged or audited.

post.summary: Admit people from a previewed group
post.description: Admits the tickets named in `ticketIds` — the people actually at the door — in one transaction, each exactly once. Every named ticket must have been admissible in the preview, else 409 `PREVIEW_MISMATCH`. Everything is re-derived under lock: the order, the group pass and its version (a replaced pass is `PREVIEW_MISMATCH`), each ticket, and the caller's authority. A ticket already admitted is reported, not refused, so a retry after a lost answer is safe. If any named ticket stopped admitting for another reason — refunded, withdrawn, handed on — nothing is admitted and the answer is 409 `GROUP_CHANGED`: look the group up again. The method follows from what was presented, as for a single ticket, and the night must be the preview's (else `PREVIEW_MISMATCH`); a ticket good for every night is admitted once on each night. Rate-limited per scanner and never cached.

get.summary: One ticket, and everywhere it has been
get.description: The ticket, the event it admits to, and every transfer it has been through in the order they happened. Read by two people with two questions — the holder asking whether it still admits them, the organiser asking whether it still should — so authorisation branches in the handler rather than on the route: the person holding it may read it, and so may anybody holding `ticket:revoke` in the organisation whose event it is. Nobody else, and a ticket belonging to somebody else answers the same way as an identifier nobody has used. The pass is not here, and neither is any transfer token: a credential is handed over once when it is derived, and a token echoed into a response is a bearer secret in a browser cache, a proxy log and a screenshot. A recipient is shown as `••••@example.com` to the holder, who sent the offer and needs to tell offers apart, and as `Hidden email` to an organiser: nothing of the local part, its length or its characters, reaches either. Names the ticket's night (`session`). The holder, and only the holder, gets an online event's `onlineJoinUrl` while the ticket admits; the organiser reading it gets null.

get.description: The bearer credential for a ticket, returned to the person holding it and to nobody else — not an organiser, not a platform administrator, not the person who bought it once they have handed it on. Safe to ask for more than once because the credential is derived rather than stored: the server recomputes `HMAC(key, ticketId:version)` and the database still holds only a SHA-256, so an attendee who closed the tab has not lost their ticket and a leaked backup is still not a set of working admissions. The derived value is checked against the stored digest before it is returned, so a pass that would not open the door is refused rather than shown. Refused for a ticket that has been transferred away, revoked, refunded, cancelled, voided or superseded, and for one whose order is not paid. Rate-limited, never cached, and never written to a log or an audit row.

post.description: Creates an invitation and returns it. The ticket does not move: TRANSFER_PENDING means somebody has been asked, and the current holder can still be admitted — an invitation nobody accepted must not leave a paying attendee at the door. A second transfer cannot start while one stands. Only the holder may offer a ticket, and a ticket bought without an account has no holder to prove a claim from. A reserved seat is offered like any other ticket and goes with it. How the one-time code reaches the recipient is `delivery.mode`: in `MANUAL`, the default, `delivery.invitationCode` is returned here exactly once, sent `no-store`, and only its digest is kept, so it can never be shown again — the sender passes it on themselves, and a lost code means withdrawing the offer and making a new one. In `EMAIL` (`DELIVERY_MODE=EMAIL` with an SMTP server configured) the code is emailed to the recipient and this carries `null`. Either way the recipient must be signed in at the offered address to use it, and the code is never logged, audited or put in the notification outbox. In `EMAIL` two limits keep this from becoming a way to email strangers: a sender may email five transfer codes an hour (429), and an address that has already been sent three codes from Desi-Event in the last day answers 429 `RECIPIENT_DAILY_LIMIT`; if the mail server refuses the message, the offer is withdrawn, the ticket is the holder’s again, and the answer is 503 `DELIVERY_FAILED`.

post.summary: Take a ticket that was offered
post.description: The old ticket becomes TRANSFERRED and its credential is cleared, so the old pass matches nothing at all rather than matching a ticket in the wrong state. A new ticket is minted for the recipient with its own credential at version one, linked to the old one so the chain from the original purchase is unbroken. A reserved seat moves with the ticket: the old row keeps the seat as history and the new one holds it, and the database allows one live ticket per seat. Accepting twice accepts once. The response carries the new pass, which is the only time it is ever returned.

sessionCookie.description: The session cookie set by `POST /v1/auth/login`. A state-changing request must also echo the `__Host-desi_csrf` cookie in the `x-desi-csrf` header and arrive from an expected origin. On a deployment served over plain HTTP the cookies lose their `__Host-` prefix.

bearerAuth.description: The same session secret `POST /v1/auth/login` returns as `token`, presented as a bearer token instead of a cookie. Opaque, not a JWT: it is the key to a session row, so revoking the session revokes the token.
